name: var vs let vs const
syntax: var x; let y; const z = 1;
description: The three ways to declare a variable in JavaScript: var is function-scoped and hoisted, while let and const are block-scoped and cannot be redeclared in the same scope.
example: if (true) { var a = 1; let b = 2; } console.log(a); // 1, b is not defined here
notes: Modern code generally avoids var in favor of let (for reassignable values) and const (the default choice).

name: Primitive Data Types
description: JavaScript has seven primitive types: string, number, boolean, undefined, null, bigint, and symbol. Primitives are immutable and compared by value.
notes: typeof null returns 'object' — a long-standing quirk of the language, not a sign that null is a reference type.

name: Reference Types (Objects)
description: Non-primitive values — objects, arrays, and functions — are reference types. Variables holding them store a reference to the value in memory, not the value itself.
example: const a = { x: 1 }; const b = a; b.x = 2; console.log(a.x); // 2, same object
notes: Assigning or passing an object copies the reference, not the data — use spread or structuredClone() to copy the actual contents.

name: Type Coercion
description: JavaScript's automatic or implicit conversion of values from one data type to another, such as during comparisons or arithmetic with mixed types.
example:
'5' + 1; // '51' (number coerced to string)
'5' - 1; // 4 (string coerced to number)
notes: Use === instead of == to avoid unexpected coercion during comparisons.

name: Truthy and Falsy Values
description: In boolean contexts, every value is either truthy or falsy. The falsy values are false, 0, -0, '', null, undefined, and NaN — everything else is truthy.
example:
if ('') { } // does not run, '' is falsy
if ('0') { } // runs, non-empty string is truthy
notes: An empty array [] and empty object {} are both truthy, which surprises many developers coming from other languages.

name: NaN
description: "Not a Number" — a special numeric value representing the result of an invalid or undefined mathematical operation.
notes: Use Number.isNaN(value) rather than isNaN(value) to avoid unwanted type coercion of non-numeric input.

name: undefined vs null
description: undefined means a variable has been declared but not assigned a value; null is an explicit assignment representing "no value" or "empty", set intentionally by a developer.
example:
let a; console.log(a); // undefined
let b = null; console.log(b); // null
notes: undefined == null is true, but undefined === null is false — they are distinct types.

name: Dynamic Typing
description: JavaScript variables are not bound to a specific type; the same variable can hold a string, then a number, then an object, over its lifetime.
example: let x = 'hello'; x = 42; x = { a: 1 }; // all valid
notes: TypeScript adds static typing on top of JavaScript's dynamic typing to catch these kinds of mismatches at compile time.

name: Number Precision (Floating Point)
description: JavaScript represents all numbers as 64-bit floating point (IEEE 754), which can cause small rounding errors in decimal arithmetic.
notes: For exact decimal math (e.g. currency), round with toFixed(), scale to integers, or use a dedicated decimal library.

name: Global Scope
description: Variables and functions declared outside any function or block live in the global scope and are accessible from anywhere in the program.
example: var globalVar = 'I am global'; function show() { console.log(globalVar); }
notes: Excessive use of global scope increases the risk of naming collisions — ES modules scope top-level declarations to the module instead.
